title: Christina Applegate misdiagnosis: Why can MS be difficult to diagnose?
summary: MS advocate Christina Applegate recently announced that her MS diagnosis was incorrect, based on new test results. Why can the disease be difficult to identify?
body: Actor Christina Applegate was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) over five years ago — but this week, she announced that a recent reevaluation found that she doesn't have the condition after all. In the wake of that revelation, she's been left without a diagnosis, and she said on a podcast that she felt she was "back at square one, where I don't know what's going on with me." Applegate's case is not totally unique, although MS diagnosis has improved over the years. Studies offer different estimates of how frequently MS is misdiagnosed, with rates ranging from 5% to over 40%, depending on the patient population and clinical setting. There is also some degree of underdiagnosis — cases in which people with MS aren't flagged as having the disease. So, how difficult is MS to identify, and what does that mean for patients? Live Science spoke with experts about the current state of MS diagnostics and the improvements that may be coming in the future. title: Could 'body clocks' play a role in depression? Study proposes a new 'circadian' subtype
summary: Researchers propose a new subtype of depression linked to body-clock patterns.
body: Some people with depression sleep far more than average, wake up exhausted, habitually stay up late, and experience mood shifts with the seasons. A new study suggests that these symptoms may cluster in a distinct subtype of depression that's tied to the body's internal clock. While research has long linked a scrambled circadian rhythm to a risk of mood disorders, neuroscientists are now proposing that these disruptions define a specific form of depression that they call "circadian depression." First conceptualized in 2021 , the body-clock subtype may affect about 1 in 4 people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, the researchers estimate. In their new study, published Wednesday (Oct. 21) in The British Journal of Psychiatry , the team identified the subtype in about 2,600 people out of over 11,000 evaluated. "Circadian depression is a biologically informed subtype," said study co-author Emiliana Tonini , a neuroscientist at the University of Sydney. "Unlike subtypes defined mainly by symptoms, the core feature here is a disturbed circadian system, which common antidepressants may not fully address," Tonini told Live Science in an email. title: Rising temperatures could boost pregnancy risks worldwide — here's how
summary: As climate change fuels extreme temperatures and makes severely hot days more frequent, doctors are concerned about the health impacts on pregnant people.
body: Rising temperatures around the globe are contributing to a range of health risks, from infectious disease to food insecurity and wildfire smoke . Extreme heat is another major public health concern, as climate change drives up both average temperatures and the frequency of extremely hot days. This August was the world's hottest on record , and it drove upticks in heat-related emergency visits and deaths in various U.S. states. Hotter weather is expected to pose dangerous health risks for millions, and pregnant people are especially vulnerable to its impacts, experts caution. "Pregnant people are physiologically more vulnerable to heat," Dr. Susanna Esposito , a pediatrician at the University of Parma in Italy, told Live Science. "Climate adaptation should treat pregnant people as a priority population." Extreme heat is linked to adverse birth outcomes that can be fatal for both mothers and newborns. Heat can also hinder fetuses' development, contributing to long-term health and cognitive effects.
